decks.title: Chemical Thermodynamics — Part 1: Systems, work, heat, internal energy and enthalpy
goals: Distinguish types of system and identify state functions
Apply the IUPAC sign convention to work and heat, and calculate expansion work
State and apply the first law, ΔU = q + w
Relate ΔH and ΔU, and use heat capacities with C_p − C_v = R

slides.heading: Chemical Thermodynamics
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how energy moves as heat and work when matter changes, and how to keep an exact account of it.

rows: How much heat is released per mole?
A cold pack cools your ankle
A piston in a petrol engine
How much work can the gas do?
Ice melts in a warm room
Why does it happen by itself?

visual.alt: Table of four everyday changes and the thermodynamic question each raises

slides.narration: Welcome. Whenever a fuel burns, a cold pack chills your ankle or ice melts on the table, energy changes form and moves around. Thermodynamics is the bookkeeping of that energy. In this part we define the terms carefully, fix the sign convention for heat and work, and meet the first law and the enthalpy, which chemists use every day.

slides.heading: System, surroundings and types of system
slides.body_md: The part of the universe we study is the **system**; everything else that can exchange energy with it is the **surroundings**. The system is separated by a **boundary**, real or imaginary.

rows: Sealed boiling tube in a water bath
Tea in a good vacuum flask (approximately)

visual.alt: Table comparing open, closed and isolated systems by exchange of matter and energy, with an example of each

slides.narration: The system is the part we choose to study, and the surroundings are everything else that can exchange energy with it. An open system exchanges both matter and energy, like tea in an open cup. A closed system exchanges only energy, like a sealed tube in a water bath. An isolated system exchanges neither, and a good vacuum flask comes close.

slides.heading: State functions and path functions
slides.body_md: A **state function** depends only on the present state of the system, not on how it got there. Heat and work are **path functions**: their values depend on the route taken.

rows: Change depends only on initial and final states
Round trip need not give zero

visual.alt: Table contrasting state functions such as U, H, S and G with path functions heat and work

slides.narration: A state function depends only on the present condition of the system. Pressure, volume, temperature, internal energy, enthalpy, entropy and Gibbs energy are state functions, so their change depends only on the start and the end. Heat and work are not. They describe how a change was made, and different routes give different amounts.

slides.heading: Extensive and intensive properties
slides.body_md: **Extensive** properties depend on the amount of matter (mass, volume, $U$, $H$, $S$, $G$). **Intensive** properties do not ($T$, $p$, density, molar quantities). The ratio of two extensive properties is intensive.

rows: Same in each half of a sample

visual.alt: Table of extensive and intensive properties with reasons

slides.narration: Cut a sample in half. Properties that halve, such as mass, volume and internal energy, are extensive. Properties that stay the same, such as temperature, pressure and density, are intensive. A handy rule: the ratio of two extensive properties, for example mass divided by volume, is always intensive.

slides.heading: Quick check: type of system
slides.body_md: Classify a system by what crosses its boundary.
slides.narration: Quick check. Ask what can cross the boundary: matter, energy, both or neither.

slides.heading: Work and heat: the IUPAC sign convention
slides.body_md: Signs are written **from the point of view of the system**. Energy entering the system is **positive**; energy leaving is **negative**. Work done **on** the system is $w > 0$; heat **absorbed** is $q > 0$.

visual.alt: Table of the IUPAC sign convention for heat and work from the system point of view

slides.narration: Always take the point of view of the system, like a bank account. Energy flowing in is a deposit and carries a positive sign; energy flowing out is a withdrawal and carries a negative sign. So when a gas expands and pushes the surroundings, the work is negative, and when the system takes in heat, the heat is positive.

slides.heading: Pressure–volume work as an area
slides.body_md: Expansion work equals the **area under the p–V curve**. Reversible expansion follows the isotherm and does the **maximum** work; a one-step irreversible expansion against a constant $p_\text{ex}$ gives a smaller rectangle.

visual.alt: Pressure against volume for one mole of ideal gas expanding from 5 litres to 20 litres at 300 kelvin: the area under the isotherm is the reversible work, the smaller rectangle is the work of a one-step irreversible expansion
visual.caption: Reversible work is the maximum work the gas can do.

slides.narration: In this picture the gas expands from five litres to twenty litres. In the one step expansion the gas pushes against a constant outside pressure, and the work is the green rectangle. If the outside pressure always matches the gas pressure, the gas follows the blue curve, and the work is the whole area beneath it. That area is larger, so reversible work is the maximum.

slides.heading: Expansion work formulas
slides.body_md: Work is calculated differently for each way of expanding. For an ideal gas at constant temperature, $\Delta U = 0$, so $q = -w$.

visual.alt: Table of formulas for expansion work for free, irreversible and reversible isothermal expansion

slides.narration: Three cases cover most questions. If the gas expands into a vacuum, the outside pressure is zero and no work is done. If it expands against a constant outside pressure, the work is minus that pressure times the change in volume. For a reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, the work is minus two point three zero three times n R T times the logarithm of the volume ratio.

slides.heading: Worked example: irreversible and reversible work
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** One mole of an ideal gas at 300 K expands from 5.0 L to 20 L. Calculate the work done by the gas (a) against a constant $p_\text{ex} = 1.25$ bar and (b) reversibly and isothermally. ($R = 8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$; $1\ \text{L bar} = 100\ \text{J}$)

**(a)** $w = -p_\text{ex}\Delta V = -1.25 \times (20 - 5.0) = -18.75\ \text{L bar} = -1875\ \text{J}$.

**(b)** $w = -2.303 \times 1 \times 8.314 \times 300 \times \log 4 = -3458\ \text{J}$, about $-3.46\ \text{kJ}$.

The reversible path does more work (3458 J against 1875 J).

visual.alt: Table comparing irreversible and reversible work for the same expansion from 5 litres to 20 litres

slides.narration: Work through it in two parts. Against the constant pressure, multiply minus one point two five bar by the fifteen litre change, giving minus eighteen point seven five litre bar, which is minus one thousand eight hundred seventy five joules. For the reversible path use the logarithm formula and get about minus three thousand four hundred fifty eight joules. The reversible route extracts more work.

slides.heading: Internal energy and the first law
slides.body_md: The **internal energy** $U$ is the total energy of the system (kinetic, potential, bonding); it is a state function. The **first law** is the conservation of energy: $\Delta U = q + w$.

visual.alt: Table of the first law applied to isolated, adiabatic, isothermal and constant volume changes

slides.narration: Internal energy is the total energy stored in a system, and the first law says it can change only by heat flowing in or work being done on it. Written as delta U equals q plus w. In an adiabatic change no heat flows, so the change equals the work. For an ideal gas at constant temperature the internal energy does not change, so heat absorbed equals work done by the gas.

slides.heading: Worked example: applying the first law
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A gas in a cylinder absorbs 650 J of heat and expands against a constant 0.80 bar from 3.0 L to 9.0 L. Find $w$ and $\Delta U$.

**Step 1.** $w = -p_\text{ex}\Delta V = -0.80 \times 6.0\ \text{L bar} = -4.8\ \text{L bar} = -480\ \text{J}$.

**Step 2.** $q = +650\ \text{J}$ (heat absorbed).

**Step 3.** $\Delta U = q + w = 650 + (-480) = +170\ \text{J}$.

visual.alt: Flow showing heat in and work out combining to give a net rise in internal energy of 170 joules

slides.narration: Take the system as the gas. It takes in six hundred fifty joules of heat, which is positive. It pushes back the surroundings, so the work is negative, minus point eight bar times six litres, which is minus four hundred eighty joules. Adding them, the internal energy rises by one hundred seventy joules.

slides.heading: Quick check: first law
slides.body_md: Apply ΔU = q + w with the correct signs.
slides.narration: Quick check. Write down the sign of heat and work from the point of view of the system before you add.

slides.heading: Enthalpy
slides.body_md: At constant pressure, heat absorbed $q_p = \Delta U + p\Delta V$. The state function **enthalpy** $H = U + pV$ gives $q_p = \Delta H$. At constant volume $q_V = \Delta U$. For reactions with gases, $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT$.

rows: Equal moles of gas on both sides
Moles of gaseous products minus reactants

visual.alt: Table relating enthalpy and internal energy changes at constant pressure and constant volume

slides.narration: Most reactions in the laboratory happen in open vessels at constant pressure, so chemists use enthalpy. Enthalpy is internal energy plus pressure times volume, and the heat absorbed at constant pressure is exactly the change in enthalpy. The two changes differ only through the gases: delta H minus delta U equals the change in moles of gas times R T.

slides.heading: Worked example: ΔH and ΔU
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** For $\ce{2SO2(g) + O2(g) -> 2SO3(g)}$, $\Delta H^\circ = -197.8\ \text{kJ}$ at 298 K. Find $\Delta U^\circ$.

**Step 1.** $\Delta n_g = 2 - 3 = -1$.

**Step 2.** $\Delta n_g RT = (-1)(8.314)(298) = -2478\ \text{J} = -2.478\ \text{kJ}$.

**Step 3.** $\Delta U = \Delta H - \Delta n_g RT = -197.8 - (-2.478) = -195.3\ \text{kJ}$.

visual.alt: Table of the quantities used to convert delta H to delta U for the oxidation of sulfur dioxide

slides.narration: Count the moles of gas. Three on the left, two on the right, so the change is minus one. Multiply by R and the temperature to get minus two point four seven eight kilojoules. Delta U is delta H minus this number, which gives minus one hundred ninety five point three kilojoules. When the volume shrinks, the surroundings do work on the system and the internal energy change is slightly less negative.

slides.heading: Heat capacity and C_p − C_v = R
slides.body_md: **Heat capacity** $C = q/\Delta T$ (extensive); **specific heat** is per gram and **molar heat capacity** per mole. At constant volume $\Delta U = nC_V\Delta T$; at constant pressure $\Delta H = nC_p\Delta T$. For an ideal gas $C_p - C_V = R$.

visual.alt: Table of molar heat capacities at constant volume and constant pressure showing a difference of R

slides.narration: Heat capacity tells us how much heat raises the temperature by one kelvin. For a gas it depends on whether the volume or the pressure is held fixed. At constant pressure the gas also does expansion work, so it needs more heat. For one mole of an ideal gas, the difference between the two molar heat capacities is exactly the gas constant R.

slides.heading: Exothermic and endothermic changes
slides.body_md: In an **exothermic** change $\Delta H < 0$: products have lower enthalpy than reactants. In an **endothermic** change $\Delta H > 0$.

In an endothermic change the products sit higher, heat is absorbed, and delta H is positive. The sign of delta H is the sign of the heat flow at constant pressure.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Open, closed and isolated systems differ in exchange of matter and energy.
State functions (p, V, T, U, H, S, G) depend only on the state; q and w are path functions.
IUPAC convention: energy into the system is positive. Expansion work is negative.
w = −p_ex ΔV (irreversible); w = −2.303 nRT log(V₂/V₁) (reversible, isothermal); ΔU = q + w.
ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT; q_p = ΔH; q_V = ΔU; C_p − C_V = R.

visual.alt: Summary table of the main relations in Part 1

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Systems are open, closed or isolated. State functions depend only on the state, while heat and work depend on the path. Using the system point of view, energy entering is positive. The first law says delta U equals q plus w, enthalpy is U plus pV, and delta H differs from delta U by the change in moles of gas times R T.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: State the sign convention before you calculate: work done by the gas is negative.
Convert units: 1 L bar = 100 J; R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ with ΔH in kJ needs ÷ 1000.
For Δn_g count only gaseous species, and use T in kelvin.
Write "state function" examples and the reason: depends only on initial and final states.
Free expansion into a vacuum: w = 0.

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Some exam tips. Say which sign convention you use, and remember that work done by the gas is negative. Convert litre bar to joules and watch the kilojoules in delta H. When you work out delta n for gases, count only the gaseous species. And do not forget that free expansion against zero pressure does no work.

decks.title: Chemical Thermodynamics — Part 2: Enthalpy of reaction, Hess’s law, entropy and Gibbs energy
goals: Measure ΔU and ΔH by bomb and constant-pressure calorimetry
Define the standard enthalpies of formation, combustion, atomisation, sublimation, phase transition, ionisation, solution and dilution
Apply Hess’s law and bond enthalpies to find ΔH of reactions
Use ΔS = q_rev/T, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS and ΔG° = −2.303RT log K to judge spontaneity and equilibrium

slides.heading: Enthalpy, Entropy and Spontaneity
slides.body_md: Part 2 — measuring heats of reaction, combining them by Hess’s law, and predicting which changes happen on their own.

rows: How much heat does a reaction give out?
Can I get an unmeasurable ΔH from known ones?
Does a reaction go by itself?

visual.alt: Table of four questions of Part 2 and the tool used to answer each

slides.narration: In this part we measure the heat of a reaction in a calorimeter, learn the named enthalpy changes, and combine them with Hess’s law. Then we ask a deeper question: why do some changes happen by themselves? Entropy and Gibbs energy give the answer, and link directly to the equilibrium constant.

slides.heading: Measuring ΔU and ΔH: calorimetry
slides.body_md: A **bomb calorimeter** is a sealed steel vessel at constant volume: it measures $\Delta U$. A **coffee-cup (open) calorimeter** is at constant pressure: it measures $\Delta H$. Heat absorbed by the calorimeter $q = C\Delta T$ or $mc\Delta T$.

rows: Constant pressure, open to the air

visual.alt: Table comparing bomb and constant-pressure calorimeters

slides.narration: A bomb calorimeter is a strong sealed vessel, so the volume stays constant and no expansion work is done. The heat it records is therefore the change in internal energy. A simple cup calorimeter is open to the air, so the pressure is constant and the heat is the enthalpy change. Heat is found from the heat capacity times the temperature rise.

slides.heading: Worked example: constant-pressure calorimetry
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** 50 mL of 1.0 M HCl is mixed with 50 mL of 1.0 M NaOH in a coffee-cup calorimeter; the temperature rises by 6.8 K (given). Take the 100 g of solution to have $c = 4.18\ \text{J g}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$. Find $\Delta H$ per mole of water formed.

**Step 1.** Heat gained by solution $= mc\Delta T = 100 \times 4.18 \times 6.8 = 2842\ \text{J}$.

**Step 2.** Moles of water formed $= 0.050\ \text{mol}$.

**Step 3.** $\Delta H = -\dfrac{2842}{0.050} = -56850\ \text{J mol}^{-1} = -56.8\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ (textbook value about −57).

visual.alt: Table of heat gained, moles of water and the enthalpy of neutralisation calculated from the calorimeter data

slides.narration: The solution warms up, so the reaction released heat. The heat gained by one hundred grams of solution is mass times specific heat times temperature rise, about two thousand eight hundred forty two joules. This came from point zero five zero mole of water forming, so the enthalpy of neutralisation is about minus fifty seven kilojoules per mole, negative because heat was released.

slides.heading: Standard enthalpy changes: formation, combustion, atomisation, sublimation
slides.body_md: The **standard state** is the pure substance at 1 bar (298 K is usual). $\Delta_f H^\circ$ is for forming **one mole** from elements in their reference states; $\Delta_f H^\circ$ of an element is **zero**.

visual.alt: Table of standard enthalpies of formation, combustion, atomisation and sublimation with an example reaction and value for each

slides.narration: Standard enthalpy changes refer to one mole under standard conditions. Formation builds one mole of a compound from its elements, and the value for an element itself is zero. Combustion burns one mole completely in oxygen and is always negative. Atomisation produces gaseous atoms, and sublimation turns a solid straight into a gas. Both of these absorb heat.

slides.heading: Phase transition, ionisation, solution and dilution
slides.body_md: **Phase transitions** (fusion, vaporisation) absorb heat. **Ionisation enthalpy** is for removing an electron from a gaseous atom. **Enthalpy of solution** is for dissolving one mole in a large excess of solvent. **Enthalpy of dilution** is for adding more solvent to a solution.

visual.alt: Table of enthalpy changes of phase transition, ionisation, solution and dilution with examples and values

slides.narration: Melting and boiling absorb heat, so their enthalpy changes are positive. Removing an electron from a gaseous sodium atom costs four hundred ninety six kilojoules per mole. Dissolving sodium hydroxide releases heat, so the solution warms, while ammonium nitrate absorbs heat and cools, which is how a cold pack works. Diluting concentrated sulfuric acid releases a great deal of heat.

slides.heading: Quick check: enthalpy terms
slides.body_md: Match a process with its enthalpy term.
slides.narration: Quick check. Decide whether the process makes one mole from elements, burns in oxygen, or breaks into atoms.

slides.heading: Hess’s law of constant heat summation
slides.body_md: The enthalpy change of a reaction is the **same whether it takes place in one step or several**, because $H$ is a state function. We can add equations and add their $\Delta H$ values; reversing an equation changes the sign; multiplying scales $\Delta H$.

visual.alt: Table of the effect on delta H of reversing, multiplying and adding thermochemical equations

slides.narration: Because enthalpy is a state function, the total change between the same start and end does not depend on the route. This lets us calculate enthalpy changes that cannot be measured directly. Add the equations to get the target, adding their enthalpy changes. Reverse an equation and the sign flips; double it and the value doubles.

slides.heading: A Hess cycle: graphite to carbon dioxide
slides.body_md: Burning carbon to $\ce{CO}$ cannot be measured cleanly, but $\Delta H$ of the second step follows from the other two by **Hess’s law**.

slides.narration: Here graphite and oxygen reach carbon dioxide by two routes. Direct burning releases three hundred ninety three point five kilojoules per mole. Alternatively, first make carbon monoxide, releasing one hundred ten point five, then burn that to carbon dioxide. The second step must release the difference, two hundred eighty three kilojoules, so both routes add up to the same total.

slides.heading: Worked example: ΔH from enthalpies of formation
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find $\Delta_r H^\circ$ for $\ce{4NH3(g) + 5O2(g) -> 4NO(g) + 6H2O(g)}$ using $\Delta_f H^\circ$ (kJ mol⁻¹): $\ce{NH3(g)}$ -46.1, $\ce{NO(g)}$ +90.3, $\ce{H2O(g)}$ -241.8, $\ce{O2(g)}$ 0.

**Step 1.** Products: $4(+90.3) + 6(-241.8) = -1089.6$.

**Step 2.** Reactants: $4(-46.1) + 5(0) = -184.4$.

**Step 3.** $\Delta_r H^\circ = -1089.6 - (-184.4) = -905.2\ \text{kJ}$ for the equation as written.

visual.alt: Table of formation enthalpies and contributions used to find the enthalpy of ammonia oxidation

slides.narration: Use products minus reactants, each multiplied by its coefficient. The products give plus three hundred sixty one point two minus one thousand four hundred fifty point eight, which is minus eleven hundred eighty nine point six. The reactants give minus one hundred eighty four point four. Subtracting gives minus nine hundred five point two kilojoules for the equation as written.

slides.heading: Worked example: ΔH_f from enthalpies of combustion
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** $\Delta_c H^\circ$: ethyne $-1299.6$, graphite $-393.5$, hydrogen $-285.8$ kJ mol⁻¹. Find $\Delta_f H^\circ$ of $\ce{C2H2(g)}$.

**Step 1.** Target: $\ce{2C(s) + H2(g) -> C2H2(g)}$.

**Step 2.** Combine: $2\Delta_cH(\text{C}) + \Delta_cH(\text{H}_2) - \Delta_cH(\text{C}_2\text{H}_2)$.

**Step 3.** $= 2(-393.5) + (-285.8) - (-1299.6) = 226.8\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

nodes.label: Ethyne burns to the same products (reversed)

visual.alt: Flow showing the elements and ethyne burning to the same products, giving the formation enthalpy of ethyne

slides.narration: Both the elements and ethyne burn to the same products, carbon dioxide and water. Burning the elements releases seven hundred eighty seven plus two hundred eighty five point eight kilojoules. Ethyne itself releases one thousand two hundred ninety nine point six. Making ethyne from its elements is the first route followed by the second, reversed, so the result is plus two hundred twenty six point eight kilojoules per mole.

slides.heading: Bond enthalpies
slides.body_md: **Bond enthalpy** is the energy needed to break one mole of a bond in the gas phase; it is always positive. For a gaseous reaction, $\Delta_r H \approx \sum (\text{bonds broken}) - \sum (\text{bonds formed})$, using **average** values.

visual.alt: Table of average bond enthalpies in kilojoules per mole

slides.narration: Breaking bonds costs energy and making bonds releases it. For a reaction between gases we add up the energy needed to break all the bonds in the reactants and subtract the energy released on forming all the bonds in the products. Because these are average values taken over many compounds, the answer is approximate.

slides.heading: Worked example: ΔH from bond enthalpies
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Estimate $\Delta H$ for $\ce{CH4(g) + 2O2(g) -> CO2(g) + 2H2O(g)}$ using the table above.

**Step 1.** Broken: $4(\text{C–H}) + 2(\text{O=O}) = 4(414) + 2(498) = 2652\ \text{kJ}$.

**Step 2.** Formed: $2(\text{C=O}) + 4(\text{O–H}) = 2(799) + 4(463) = 3450\ \text{kJ}$.

**Step 3.** $\Delta H = 2652 - 3450 = -798\ \text{kJ}$ (the value from formation enthalpies is −802 kJ).

visual.alt: Table of bonds broken and formed in the combustion of methane with energy totals

slides.narration: Count the bonds. Methane has four carbon hydrogen bonds and each oxygen molecule has one double bond, so breaking them costs two thousand six hundred fifty two kilojoules. The products have two carbon oxygen double bonds and four oxygen hydrogen bonds, releasing three thousand four hundred fifty. The difference is minus seven hundred ninety eight, close to the value from formation data.

slides.heading: Entropy and the second law
slides.body_md: **Entropy** $S$ measures the disorder (number of ways of arranging energy and matter) of a system; it is a state function. For a reversible process $\Delta S = q_\text{rev}/T$. **Second law:** the total entropy of the system and surroundings increases in a spontaneous process.

rows: Reaction with more moles of gas

visual.alt: Table of changes that increase or decrease the entropy of a system

slides.narration: Entropy measures how spread out the energy and matter of a system are. Gases have more entropy than liquids, and liquids more than solids. When a reversible heat change takes place at constant temperature, the entropy change is the heat divided by the temperature. The second law states that the total entropy of system and surroundings rises in any spontaneous process.

slides.heading: Worked example: entropy of fusion and vaporisation
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** $\Delta_\text{fus}H = 6.01\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ at 273.15 K and $\Delta_\text{vap}H = 40.7\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ at 373 K for water. Find $\Delta S$ for each.

**Step 1.** At the transition temperature the process is reversible, so $\Delta S = \Delta H/T$.

**Step 2.** $\Delta_\text{fus}S = \dfrac{6010}{273.15} = 22.0\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$.

**Step 3.** $\Delta_\text{vap}S = \dfrac{40700}{373} = 109.1\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$; vaporisation gives the larger increase in disorder.

visual.alt: Table of enthalpy, temperature and entropy changes for fusion and vaporisation of water

slides.narration: At the melting point and the boiling point, the change happens reversibly, so entropy change equals the enthalpy change divided by the temperature. Melting one mole of ice raises the entropy by about twenty two joules per kelvin. Boiling raises it by about one hundred nine. Turning a liquid into a vapour creates far more disorder than turning a solid into a liquid.

slides.heading: Gibbs energy and spontaneity
slides.body_md: The **Gibbs energy** combines both tendencies at constant $T$ and $p$: $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$. A process is **spontaneous** if $\Delta G < 0$, at **equilibrium** if $\Delta G = 0$, and non-spontaneous if $\Delta G > 0$.

visual.alt: Table of the four sign combinations of delta H and delta S and the resulting spontaneity

slides.narration: Nature favours lower energy and higher disorder, and Gibbs energy balances the two. Delta G equals delta H minus T delta S. If it is negative the change is spontaneous. If the enthalpy change is negative and the entropy change positive, the process always goes. If both have the same sign, the temperature decides which wins.

The line falls as temperature rises, because the entropy term grows, and it crosses zero at about eleven hundred kelvin. Above that temperature the decomposition is spontaneous, which is why lime kilns run very hot.

slides.heading: Worked example: temperature of spontaneity
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** For $\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$, $\Delta H^\circ = +178.3\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $\Delta S^\circ = +160.5\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$ (assume both are independent of $T$). (a) Find $\Delta G^\circ$ at 298 K. (b) Find the minimum temperature for spontaneity.

**(a)** $\Delta G^\circ = 178.3 - 298 \times 0.1605 = 130.5\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$; positive, so not spontaneous.

**(b)** $\Delta G^\circ = 0$ at $T = \dfrac{\Delta H}{\Delta S} = \dfrac{178300}{160.5} = 1111\ \text{K}$.

visual.alt: Table of Gibbs energy change of calcium carbonate decomposition at three temperatures

slides.narration: At room temperature the entropy term is small, so delta G is positive, about one hundred thirty point five kilojoules per mole. Setting delta G to zero gives the switching temperature: delta H divided by delta S. Be careful with units, as the enthalpy is in kilojoules and the entropy in joules. The answer is about eleven hundred eleven kelvin.

slides.heading: ΔG° and the equilibrium constant
slides.body_md: At equilibrium $\Delta G = 0$, which leads to $\Delta G^\circ = -2.303\,RT\log K$. A large negative $\Delta G^\circ$ means $K \gg 1$ (products favoured); a positive $\Delta G^\circ$ means $K < 1$.

visual.alt: Table linking the sign of standard Gibbs energy change to the equilibrium constant

slides.narration: Gibbs energy also tells us how far a reaction goes. The standard Gibbs energy change equals minus two point three zero three R T times the logarithm of the equilibrium constant. If delta G naught is negative, the logarithm is positive and K is greater than one, so products are favoured. A positive value means reactants are favoured at equilibrium.

slides.heading: Quick check: spontaneity
slides.body_md: Use ΔG = ΔH − TΔS to judge spontaneity.
slides.narration: Quick check. Look at the signs of the enthalpy and entropy changes, and think about temperature.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Bomb calorimeter: ΔU at constant V; coffee-cup: ΔH at constant p.
Δ_fH° of an element is zero; Δ_rH° = Σ Δ_fH°(products) − Σ Δ_fH°(reactants).
Hess’s law: ΔH is path independent; reverse changes sign, multiplication scales.
Bond enthalpy: Δ_rH ≈ Σ broken − Σ formed (gases, average values).
ΔS = q_rev/T; ΔG = ΔH − TΔS < 0 for spontaneous change; ΔG° = −2.303 RT log K.

visual.alt: Summary table of main relations in Part 2

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Calorimeters measure heats of reaction, at constant volume for internal energy and at constant pressure for enthalpy. Hess’s law and tables of formation enthalpies let us calculate unmeasurable values, and bond enthalpies give estimates for gases. Entropy measures disorder, Gibbs energy decides spontaneity, and its standard value fixes the equilibrium constant.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2

Multiply Δ_fH° by the coefficients; elements in standard states are zero.
In ΔG = ΔH − TΔS convert ΔS from J to kJ, and T to kelvin.
Give the Gibbs-energy sign table with a reason for each case.

sections.heading: 1. System, surroundings and state functions
sections.body_md:
The **system** is the part of the universe under study; the **surroundings** exchange energy with it across a **boundary**.

- **Open:** exchanges matter and energy (tea in an open cup).
- **Closed:** exchanges energy only (a sealed tube in a water bath).
- **Isolated:** exchanges neither (an ideal vacuum flask).

**State functions** ($p, V, T, U, H, S, G$) depend only on the present state, so their changes depend only on the initial and final states. **Path functions** ($q$, $w$) depend on the route.

**Extensive** properties depend on the amount ($m, V, U, H, S, G$); **intensive** ones do not ($T, p$, density, molar quantities). The ratio of two extensive properties is intensive.

key_terms.definition_md: A property whose value depends only on the state of the system, not on the path by which it was reached.
A system that exchanges neither matter nor energy with its surroundings.
A property that does not depend on the amount of substance, such as temperature or density.

visual.alt: Types of thermodynamic system

sections.heading: 2. Work, heat and the first law
sections.body_md:
**IUPAC sign convention:** viewed from the system, energy entering is positive. Work done **on** the system: $w > 0$. Work done **by** the system (expansion): $w < 0$. Heat absorbed: $q > 0$.

**Pressure–volume work:**
- Free expansion into vacuum: $w = 0$.
- Constant external pressure: $w = -p_\text{ex}\Delta V$ ($1\ \text{L bar} = 100\ \text{J}$).
- Isothermal reversible, ideal gas: $w = -2.303\,nRT\log(V_2/V_1)$; this is the **maximum** work obtainable.

**First law:** $\Delta U = q + w$. For an isolated system $\Delta U = 0$; for an adiabatic change $\Delta U = w$; for an isothermal change of an ideal gas $\Delta U = 0$, so $q = -w$.

key_terms.definition_md: Total energy of a system: kinetic, potential and bonding energy of its particles. A state function.
A process carried out infinitely slowly so that the system is always in equilibrium with its surroundings.
A process in which no heat is exchanged, q = 0.

sections.heading: 3. Enthalpy and heat capacity
sections.body_md:
**Enthalpy** $H = U + pV$ is a state function. At constant pressure $q_p = \Delta H$; at constant volume $q_V = \Delta U$.

For reactions involving gases: $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT$, where $\Delta n_g$ is moles of gaseous products minus moles of gaseous reactants. If $\Delta n_g = 0$, $\Delta H = \Delta U$.

**Heat capacity** $C = q/\Delta T$ (extensive); molar heat capacity per mole, specific heat per gram. $\Delta U = nC_V\Delta T$, $\Delta H = nC_p\Delta T$, and for an ideal gas $C_p - C_V = R$.

**Exothermic:** $\Delta H < 0$ (products lower in enthalpy). **Endothermic:** $\Delta H > 0$.

key_terms.definition_md: H = U + pV; the heat absorbed at constant pressure equals its change.
Heat needed to raise the temperature of a system by one kelvin.

sections.heading: 4. Calorimetry and standard enthalpy changes
sections.body_md:
**Bomb calorimeter** (constant volume) measures $\Delta U$; $q = C_\text{cal}\Delta T$; then convert with $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT$. A **constant-pressure (coffee-cup) calorimeter** measures $\Delta H$: $q = mc\Delta T$.

Standard enthalpy changes (per mole, 1 bar, usually 298 K):
- **Formation** $\Delta_fH^\circ$: one mole of compound from elements in reference states; zero for an element.
- **Combustion** $\Delta_cH^\circ$: one mole burnt completely in oxygen; always negative.
- **Atomisation** $\Delta_aH^\circ$: one mole of gaseous atoms from the element (or compound).
- **Sublimation**, **fusion**, **vaporisation** (phase transitions): positive.
- **Ionisation enthalpy:** removing one electron from a gaseous atom (Na: +496 kJ mol⁻¹).
- **Solution:** dissolving one mole in a large excess of solvent (NaOH −44.5, NH₄NO₃ +25.7 kJ mol⁻¹).
- **Dilution:** enthalpy change on adding solvent to a solution.
- **Neutralisation** of a strong acid and strong base: about −57 kJ per mole of water.

key_terms.definition_md: Pure substance at 1 bar pressure; 298 K is the usual reference temperature.
Enthalpy change when one mole of a substance burns completely in oxygen under standard conditions.

sections.heading: 5. Hess’s law and bond enthalpies
sections.body_md:
**Hess’s law:** the enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whether it occurs in one step or in several, because $H$ is a state function. Reversing an equation changes the sign of $\Delta H$; multiplying scales it; equations and enthalpies can be added.

$$\Delta_rH^\circ = \sum \Delta_fH^\circ(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta_fH^\circ(\text{reactants})$$

**Bond enthalpy** is the energy to break one mole of a bond in the gas phase (average value for many compounds). For gaseous reactions, $\Delta_rH \approx \sum(\text{bonds broken}) - \sum(\text{bonds formed})$. Typical values (kJ mol⁻¹): H–H 436, C–H 414, C–C 347, C=C 611, O=O 498, O–H 463, C=O (CO₂) 799, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431.

key_terms.definition_md: The total enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the route between the same initial and final states.
Energy needed to break one mole of a particular bond in gaseous molecules; an average over compounds.

sections.heading: 6. Entropy, Gibbs energy and spontaneity
sections.body_md:
**Entropy** $S$ is a measure of disorder, a state function. For a reversible process $\Delta S = q_\text{rev}/T$. Entropy rises on melting, boiling, dissolving and when the number of gas moles increases. **Second law:** $\Delta S_\text{total} = \Delta S_\text{sys} + \Delta S_\text{surr} > 0$ for a spontaneous process.

**Gibbs energy:** $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$ (constant $T$, $p$). $\Delta G < 0$: spontaneous; $= 0$: equilibrium; $> 0$: non-spontaneous.

| ΔH | ΔS | Spontaneous? |
|---|---|---|
| − | + | At all temperatures |
| + | − | At no temperature |
| − | − | At low temperatures |
| + | + | At high temperatures |

**Equilibrium:** $\Delta G^\circ = -2.303\,RT\log K$. If $\Delta G^\circ < 0$, $K > 1$.

key_terms.definition_md: A state function measuring the disorder of a system; for a reversible change, ΔS = q_rev/T.
G = H − TS; its decrease at constant T and p is the criterion of spontaneity.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing w = +pΔV for an expansion (the work done by the gas is negative).
- Forgetting that 1 L bar = 100 J, or mixing J and kJ in ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.
- Counting solids and liquids in Δn_g (only gases count).
- Taking formed minus broken for bond enthalpies (it is broken minus formed).
- Not multiplying ΔfH° by the stoichiometric coefficients; forgetting that ΔfH° of an element is zero.
- Quoting spontaneity from ΔH alone.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: sign convention, state function or the correct relation.
- Numericals (2–3 marks): formula (½–1), substitution with units (1), answer with sign and unit (½–1).
- Reasoning (2–3 marks): the relation used and the argument in terms of ΔH, ΔS and T.

questions.stem_md: A student seals a few millilitres of ethanol in a thick glass tube and warms it in a water bath. Heat flows in, but no ethanol can escape. The ethanol in the tube is best described as:
questions.solution_md: Energy (heat) crosses the boundary but matter does not, so it is a closed system — option (d). An open system would also exchange matter; an isolated system would exchange nothing.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following quantities is a path function?

options.text_md: Heat absorbed by a gas in a change of state

questions.solution_md: U, H and S depend only on the state of the system. Heat depends on how the change is carried out, so it is a path function — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which pair contains only intensive properties?
questions.solution_md: Density (mass ÷ volume) and molar volume (volume ÷ amount) are ratios of extensive properties, so they do not depend on the amount of substance — option (c). The other pairs contain extensive quantities.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** For an ideal gas expanding isothermally, ΔU is zero even though work is done by the gas.

**Reason (R):** The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. With no change in temperature there is no change in the internal energy of an ideal gas, so q = −w; R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Molar enthalpy of vaporisation is an extensive property because enthalpy is extensive.
questions.solution_md: False. Enthalpy is extensive, but dividing it by the amount of substance gives a molar quantity, which is intensive.

questions.stem_md: A piston does 250 J of work on a gas while 90 J of heat flows out of the gas to the surroundings. The change in internal energy of the gas is:
questions.solution_md: Work done on the gas is $w = +250$ J and heat lost is $q = -90$ J, so $\Delta U = q + w = -90 + 250 = +160$, in joules — option (d). (a) ignores that heat was lost, (b) reverses the sign of the result and (c) treats both terms as losses.

questions.stem_md: One mole of an ideal gas expands isothermally into an evacuated container. For this change:
questions.solution_md: The gas pushes against zero external pressure, so w = 0. An ideal gas at constant temperature has ΔU = 0, hence q = −w = 0 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: One mole of an ideal gas expands isothermally from 5 L to 20 L, first reversibly and then in one step against the final pressure. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: The gas does more work in the irreversible expansion.
The gas does more work, and absorbs more heat, in the reversible expansion.
The work is the same, since the initial and final states are the same.
The internal energy changes by different amounts in the two expansions.

questions.solution_md: Work is a path function. The reversible path follows the isotherm, so its area under the p–V curve is the largest. Because ΔU = 0 in both cases, q = −w is also larger — option (b). ΔU is a state function and is the same (zero) for both.

questions.stem_md: An ideal gas in an insulated cylinder expands against a constant external pressure. Its temperature:

options.text_md: stays constant, because ΔU = 0 for ideal gases
cannot be predicted without the amount of gas
falls, because the work done by the gas is taken from its internal energy

questions.solution_md: The insulation makes q = 0, so ΔU = w, and w is negative for an expansion. The internal energy falls, so the temperature falls — option (d). ΔU = 0 holds only at constant temperature.

questions.stem_md: For which of the following reactions at constant temperature is $\Delta H = \Delta U$?
questions.solution_md: $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT$, so they are equal only if $\Delta n_g = 0$. The first reaction has 2 mol of gas on each side — option (c). The others have $\Delta n_g = -2$, $+1$ and $+1$.

questions.stem_md: For $\ce{N2O4(g) -> 2NO2(g)}$ at 298 K, how does $\Delta H$ compare with $\Delta U$?

options.text_md: $\Delta H$ is smaller than $\Delta U$ by $RT$
$\Delta H$ is larger than $\Delta U$ by $2RT$
$\Delta H$ is larger than $\Delta U$ by $RT$

questions.solution_md: $\Delta n_g = 2 - 1 = +1$, so $\Delta H - \Delta U = \Delta n_g RT = +RT$ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The molar heat capacity of dinitrogen at constant pressure is $29.1\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$. Treating it as an ideal gas ($R = 8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$), its $C_V$ is about:
questions.solution_md: $C_V = C_p - R = 29.1 - 8.314 = 20.8$, in $\text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$ — option (a). (b) adds $R$ instead of subtracting it.

questions.stem_md: A fuel is burnt in a sealed, rigid steel bomb surrounded by water. The temperature rise of the water gives directly:

options.text_md: the change in internal energy, ΔU
the work done by the gases, w

questions.solution_md: The volume is fixed, so no expansion work is done (w = 0) and q_V = ΔU — option (b). ΔH is then calculated using ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The heat absorbed by a system at constant pressure has a definite value for a given change of state.

**Reason (R):** At constant pressure the heat absorbed equals the change in enthalpy, which is a state function.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. Heat in general is a path function, but under the single condition of constant pressure it equals ΔH, so it depends only on the initial and final states; R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The work done by a gas in free expansion into a vacuum is large, because the gas expands very rapidly.

**Reason (R):** In free expansion the external pressure is zero.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: with p_ex = 0, w = −p_ex ΔV = 0, whatever the speed of expansion. R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** $\Delta H$ and $\Delta U$ differ for $\ce{N2(g) + 3H2(g) -> 2NH3(g)}$.

**Reason (R):** $\Delta n_g$ is zero for this reaction.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true because $\Delta n_g = 2 - 4 = -2$, so $\Delta H - \Delta U = -2RT$. R is false (Δn_g is −2, not zero) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The temperature of an ideal gas does not change when it expands freely into a vacuum.
questions.solution_md: True. Here w = 0 and, with no heat exchange, ΔU = 0; for an ideal gas the internal energy depends only on temperature, so T is unchanged.

questions.stem_md: A bomb calorimeter measures the change in ___ energy of a reaction directly.
questions.solution_md: At constant volume the heat exchanged is q_V = ΔU, the change in **internal** energy.

questions.stem_md: Calculate the work, in joules, done by $0.5\ \text{mol}$ of an ideal gas when it expands reversibly and isothermally at $300\ \text{K}$ from $2\ \text{L}$ to $10\ \text{L}$. ($R = 8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution_md: $w = -2.303\,nRT\log\dfrac{V_2}{V_1} = -2.303 \times 0.5 \times 8.314 \times 300 \times \log 5 = -2007$, so $-2007\ \text{J}$ (the gas does work, so $w$ is negative).

questions.stem_md: The enthalpy change for the process $\ce{CH4(g) -> C(g) + 4H(g)}$ is called the standard enthalpy of:
questions.solution_md: The molecule is completely broken into gaseous atoms: that is atomisation — option (b). Formation starts from the elements in their reference states; combustion needs oxygen.

questions.stem_md: At 298 K and 1 bar, the standard enthalpy of formation is zero for:
questions.solution_md: ΔfH° is zero for an element in its most stable (reference) form. At 298 K bromine is a liquid, so Br₂(l) — option (a). Gaseous bromine, diamond and ozone are not the most stable forms.

questions.stem_md: Which standard enthalpy change is always negative?
questions.solution_md: Burning a substance completely in oxygen always releases heat — option (d). Atomisation and fusion absorb heat; the enthalpy of solution may have either sign.

questions.stem_md: The heat released on neutralising a strong acid with a strong base is about 57 kJ per mole of water, but it is smaller when ethanoic acid is neutralised with sodium hydroxide. The reason is that:

options.text_md: some of the energy is used to ionise the weak acid completely
ethanoic acid is a stronger acid than the strong acids
water is not formed in this reaction

questions.solution_md: Ionisation of a weak acid absorbs energy, which offsets part of the heat released when H⁺ and OH⁻ combine — option (a). Water is still formed, and the overall reaction is still exothermic.

questions.stem_md: The enthalpy change on dissolving one mole of a substance in a very large amount of solvent is the enthalpy of ___.
questions.solution_md: This defines the enthalpy of **solution**.

questions.stem_md: Given $\ce{S(s) + O2(g) -> SO2(g)}$, $\Delta H = -296.8\ \text{kJ}$ and $\ce{SO2(g) + 1/2O2(g) -> SO3(g)}$, $\Delta H = -98.9\ \text{kJ}$ (given), the enthalpy of formation of $\ce{SO3(g)}$ from sulfur and oxygen is:
questions.solution_md: Adding the two equations gives $\ce{S(s) + 3/2O2(g) -> SO3(g)}$, so $\Delta H = -296.8 + (-98.9) = -395.7$, in kJ mol⁻¹ — option (c). (a) subtracts the second value instead of adding.

questions.stem_md: Using bond enthalpies (H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431, all in kJ mol⁻¹), the enthalpy change for $\ce{H2(g) + Cl2(g) -> 2HCl(g)}$ is:
questions.solution_md: Bonds broken: $436 + 242 = 678$; bonds formed: $2 \times 431 = 862$. $\Delta H = 678 - 862 = -184$, in kJ — option (b). (a) subtracts the wrong way round.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The standard enthalpy of formation of O₂(g) at 298 K is zero.

**Reason (R):** Enthalpy is a state function.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but R does not explain A. ΔfH° of an element in its reference state is zero **by definition** (forming an element from itself involves no change) — option (b).

answer.model_answer_md: Products: $3(-393.5) = -1180.5$ kJ; Fe(s) is an element, so 0. Reactants: $-824.2 + 3(-110.5) = -1155.7$ kJ. $\Delta H^\circ = -1180.5 - (-1155.7) = -24.80$ kJ. It is negative, so the reaction is exothermic.

questions.solution_md: $\Delta_rH^\circ = \sum\Delta_fH^\circ(\text{P}) - \sum\Delta_fH^\circ(\text{R}) = -1180.5 - (-1155.7) = -24.80$, in kJ.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State Hess’s law and explain why it holds.

(b) Given the enthalpies of combustion of graphite (−393.5), hydrogen (−285.8) and methane (−890.3 kJ mol⁻¹), calculate the enthalpy of formation of methane.

(c) Mention two uses of Hess’s law.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Hess’s law states that the enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whether it occurs in one step or in several steps, because enthalpy is a state function. (b) Required: $\ce{C(s) + 2H2(g) -> CH4(g)}$. $\Delta_fH = \Delta_cH(\text{C}) + 2\Delta_cH(\text{H}_2) - \Delta_cH(\text{CH}_4) = -393.5 + 2(-285.8) - (-890.3) = -74.80$ kJ mol⁻¹. (c) It lets us find enthalpy changes that cannot be measured directly, such as formation of methane or carbon monoxide, and it allows lattice or bond enthalpies to be calculated from cycles.

questions.solution_md: Statement and reason; combination of combustion data; two uses.

questions.stem_md: Define each of the following and give an equation or example: (a) standard enthalpy of formation, (b) standard enthalpy of combustion, (c) enthalpy of atomisation, (d) enthalpy of sublimation, (e) enthalpy of solution. Mention the usual sign of each.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound forms from its elements in their reference states, e.g. $\ce{H2(g) + 1/2O2(g) -> H2O(l)}$, −285.8 kJ mol⁻¹; usually negative. (b) The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance burns completely in oxygen, e.g. graphite, −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹; always negative. (c) The enthalpy change to convert one mole of a substance into gaseous atoms, e.g. $\ce{1/2H2(g) -> H(g)}$, +218 kJ mol⁻¹; positive. (d) The enthalpy change when one mole of a solid changes directly to vapour, e.g. iodine, +62 kJ mol⁻¹; positive. (e) The enthalpy change when one mole dissolves in a large excess of solvent; negative for NaOH, positive for NH₄NO₃.

questions.solution_md: One definition, example and sign for each of the five terms.

questions.stem_md: For $\ce{N2(g) + 3H2(g) -> 2NH3(g)}$, $\Delta H = -92\ \text{kJ}$ and $\Delta S = -199\ \text{J K}^{-1}$. The reaction is spontaneous:

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between a state function and a path function. Give one example of each.

questions.stem_md: Why is ΔH almost equal to ΔU for reactions involving only solids and liquids?

answer.model_answer_md: $\Delta H = \Delta U + p\Delta V$. For solids and liquids the volume change is very small, so $p\Delta V$ is negligible, and there are no moles of gas, so $\Delta n_g RT = 0$. Hence ΔH ≈ ΔU.

questions.stem_md: Using a p–V graph, explain why the work obtained from a reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas is greater than that from a one-step irreversible expansion between the same states.

In the one-step expansion the gas works against the lower final pressure, giving only a smaller rectangle. Hence reversible work is the maximum.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State the first law of thermodynamics and write its mathematical form with the IUPAC sign convention.

(b) Write the values of q, w and ΔU (or their relation) for (i) an isolated system, (ii) an adiabatic change, (iii) an isothermal change of an ideal gas.

(c) A gas absorbs 50 J of heat and 30 J of work is done on it. Find ΔU.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; the change in internal energy equals heat absorbed plus work done on the system: $\Delta U = q + w$, where q and w are positive when energy enters the system. (b) (i) Isolated: q = 0, w = 0, ΔU = 0. (ii) Adiabatic: q = 0, so ΔU = w. (iii) Isothermal for an ideal gas: ΔU = 0, so q = −w. (c) $q = +50$ J and $w = +30$ J, so $\Delta U = 50 + 30 = +80$ J.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define enthalpy and show that the heat absorbed at constant pressure equals ΔH.

(b) Derive ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT.

(c) For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) at 298 K, ΔH = −92.2 kJ. State whether ΔH is larger or smaller than ΔU and by how much.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Enthalpy is a state function defined as $H = U + pV$. By the first law, $\Delta U = q_p + w$ with $w = -p\Delta V$ at constant pressure, so $q_p = \Delta U + p\Delta V$. This is the change in $U + pV$, which is $\Delta H$; hence the heat absorbed at constant pressure equals the enthalpy change. (b) For gases, $p\Delta V = \Delta n_g RT$ from $pV = nRT$ at constant T, so $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT$. (c) Here $\Delta n_g = 2 - 4 = -2$, so $\Delta H - \Delta U = -2RT = -2 \times 8.314 \times 298 = -4955$ J, i.e. about −4.96 kJ. ΔH is therefore smaller (more negative) than ΔU by about 4.96 kJ, because the volume of the gaseous system shrinks and the surroundings do work on it.

(a) Write the Gibbs equation and the criterion of spontaneity.

(b) Explain, for the four combinations of signs of ΔH and ΔS, the temperatures at which a reaction is spontaneous.

(c) How is ΔG° related to the equilibrium constant? What does a large negative ΔG° imply?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$; a process at constant T and p is spontaneous if ΔG < 0, at equilibrium if ΔG = 0. (b) ΔH negative, ΔS positive: ΔG is always negative, so spontaneous at all temperatures. ΔH positive, ΔS negative: ΔG always positive, so never spontaneous. Both negative: spontaneous only at low T. Both positive: spontaneous only at high T. (c) $\Delta G^\circ = -2.303\,RT\log K$. A large negative ΔG° gives a large K, so the products are strongly favoured at equilibrium.
